articles.content: From Helsinki to Istanbul, independent developers are putting Grand Theft Auto-style action on their home streets, and without billion-dollar budgets. They tell us how they do it Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle. He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. Rockstar’s 3D open world template, it turned out, could be plonked in just about any location, so long as it had people and enough cars to run them over with. After GTA III attracted immense commercial success (and controversy), dozens of copycats and spiritual sequels hit the market throughout the 00s and 2010s. Gamers had a pithy name for them: “GTA clones”. Continue reading...

articles.content: We put 11 range extenders and mesh systems to the test to find the fastest and most reliable for streaming, gaming and working from home • The best office chairs Fast fibre broadband is fantastic – if the wifi signal reaches the part of your home where you need it. Most of us use the router provided by our broadband provider, often tucked away in a hallway or corner of the lounge. Sadly, these often don’t have the range to cover every room in your home, leaving you high and dry when you’re trying to binge-watch TV or get work done in a distant home office. Wifi extenders and mesh systems can help. Extenders plug in to a mains socket between your location and the router, then pass data backwards and forwards to extend your router’s reach. Mesh systems are even smarter, pairing a secondary router with one or two satellite units, which work together to extend the wifi coverage throughout your home. The mesh system can pass your connection from unit to unit to make sure you’re always getting the best possible link from your device to the internet, wherever you are in your home. articles.content: Life100 features the wisdom of two women in their 80s and has gone viral by exploring important life lessons It is, unfortunately, a familiar scene. At the dinner table, a woman berates her granddaughter with invasive, personal questions – why are you still single? articles.content: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. Continue reading...

articles.content: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.content: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. Continue reading...

articles.content: The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. articles.content: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. Continue reading...
